title: Area VI review: Navigation
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area VI: pilotage and dead reckoning, navigation systems and radar services, diversion, and lost procedures. Many are real cross-country scenarios that join two Tasks.

questions.q: A student's planning sheet reads: TC 112°, WCA 5° L (wind from the left), TH 107°, variation 3° W, MH 104°, deviation -1°, CH 103°. Which step is wrong?
options: The WCA step: a wind from the left should be added to the true course to get the heading
The deviation step: deviation is always added, so the compass heading should be 105°
None; the compass heading of 103° is right, since every step was worked in the correct order
The variation step: west variation is added, so MH should be 110° and CH 109°
questions.why: Wind from the left is subtracted, so TH 107° is right [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. West variation is added (west is best), so MH = 110°, and deviation -1° gives CH 109° [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]] [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]. Deviation is added or subtracted as the card shows.

questions.q: You are heading 210°. You turn the OBS until the needle centers, and the course index reads 030 with a FROM flag. Where are you?
options: On the 030 radial, northeast of the station, flying toward it
On the 210 radial, southwest of the station, flying away from it
On the 030 radial, flying away from the station, because the flag shows FROM
You can't tell your radial until you turn to a heading of 030°
questions.why: Centered with FROM, the OBS shows the radial you are on: 030, northeast of the station [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. The VOR does not care about your heading, and TO/FROM does not show which way the nose points [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. With the nose on 210°, you are pointed back toward the station.

questions.q: You decide to divert. On the chart the new true course is 184°. The isogonic line shows 8° E variation. You will cruise more than 3,000 ft above the ground. Which altitude fits the VFR cruising rule?
options: 5,500 ft MSL
4,500 ft MSL
6,500 ft MSL
5,000 ft MSL
questions.why: The rule uses magnetic course. East is least: 184 - 8 = 176° magnetic [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Courses of 0° to 179° use odd thousands + 500, so 5,500 ft [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. The true course alone would point you to the wrong (even) altitude.

questions.q: You are unsure of your position. You see a small town with a racetrack. A town on the chart about 6 miles left of your course also has a racetrack, so you are tempted to call it a fix. What should you do?
options: Accept it as a fix, since a racetrack is a rare feature and the match to the chart looks good
Confirm it with other features, such as roads, rivers or railroads, before you trust it
Ignore landmarks for now and wait for the next radio fix before you decide where you are
Turn toward that town right away on the chance that it is the one on the chart, to get back on course
questions.why: Good checkpoints can be confirmed by other features, and you should never place complete reliance on any single checkpoint [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Forcing one feature to fit the chart is how pilots get more lost. Turning away from your heading on a guess also makes it easy to get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

questions.q: You fly over the airborne VOR checkpoint listed for the 220 radial. The needle centers with the OBS on 225 and a FROM flag. How does this receiver do?
options: Not good: the most error allowed on any check is ±4°
Not good: an airborne check allows only ±2°
Good: 5° is inside the ±6° limit for an airborne check
You can't tell, because airborne checks must be read with a TO flag
questions.why: The error is 225 - 220 = 5°. The airborne checkpoint limit is ±6°; ±4° is the limit for a VOT or a ground checkpoint [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]]. For VFR the check is not required, but PHAK suggests using these IFR limits [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].

questions.q: Your vacuum pump quits and the heading indicator is useless. You are flying west at about 44° N latitude when ATC says: 'Turn right heading 360.' On the magnetic compass, where should you stop the turn?
options: When the compass reads about 323°
When the compass reads about 037°
When the compass reads about 338°
When the compass reads 360°
questions.why: Turning to north, the compass leads, so stop the turn early by 15° plus half the latitude: 15 + 22 = 37°. 360 - 37 = 323° [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. Going past the heading is the rule for turns to south.

questions.q: It will be dark when you land at your diversion airport. Its sectional data block reads '1150 L 38 122.7'. Which statement is correct?
options: Field elevation 1,150 ft, lighting sunset to sunrise, longest runway about 3,800 ft (usable length may be less), UNICOM 122.7
Pattern altitude 1,150 ft AGL, lights only on request, runway 380 ft long, CTAF 122.7
Field elevation 1,150 ft, lighting with limits (see the Chart Supplement), longest runway 3,800 ft, tower 122.7
Field elevation 115 ft, lighting sunset to sunrise, longest runway 1,150 ft, UNICOM 122.7
questions.why: The block gives elevation, then lighting (L = sunset to sunrise; *L would mean limits), then the longest runway in hundreds of feet, usable length may be less, then UNICOM [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide, Airports]]. Lighting codes refer to runway edge lights and may not be for the longest runway, so check the Chart Supplement before a night arrival [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide, Airports]].

questions.q: Lost, you tune and identify two VORs. On VOR X the needle centers with the OBS on 200 and a TO flag. On VOR Y it centers with the OBS on 110 and a FROM flag. Which lines do you draw to find your position?
options: The 200 radial of X and the 110 radial of Y
The 020 radial of X and the 110 radial of Y
The 200 radial of X and the 290 radial of Y
The 020 radial of X and the 290 radial of Y
questions.why: With a TO flag the OBS shows the course to the station, so you are on the reciprocal radial: 200 TO means the 020 radial. With FROM, the OBS is your radial: 110 [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Draw both radials out from their stations; you are where they cross [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

questions.q: A classmate filled in a 69 NM leg on the nav log as 36 minutes and 4.8 gallons, using the 115-knot TAS. The winds aloft give a 92-knot groundspeed, and the burn is 8 GPH. What should the log say?
options: 36 minutes and 4.8 gallons
36 minutes and 6.0 gallons
45 minutes and 4.8 gallons
45 minutes and 6.0 gallons
questions.why: Time = distance ÷ GS: 69 ÷ 92 = 0.75 hr = 45 minutes [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Fuel = 0.75 × 8 = 6.0 gallons. With wind, use GS, not TAS; using TAS gives the too-small 36 minutes and 4.8 gallons [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

questions.q: You are on flight following, holding your course with the nose about 15° to the right because of a wind from the right. ATC says: 'Traffic 12 o'clock, 4 miles, opposite direction.' Where do you look first?
options: Straight over the nose, since the traffic is called at 12 o'clock
A little left of the nose, between 11 and 12 o'clock
Off the right wingtip, about 3 o'clock
A little right of the nose, between 12 and 1 o'clock
questions.why: ATC calls traffic from your track, not your heading, so a crab changes where you see it [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]] [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15]]. Your nose points 15° right of your track, so traffic straight ahead on your track is 15° left of the nose. One clock hour is 30°, so that is between 11 and 12 o'clock. In the figure, airplane B also has the wind from the right, and its pilot also sees the traffic left of the nose (at 10 o'clock, because B crabs more).

questions.q: You are directly over a VOR when you decide to divert. The alternate airport is 15 NM out on that VOR's 075 radial. How do you set up the VOR to fly there?
options: OBS on 255, and fly it with a TO flag
OBS on 075, and fly it with a TO flag
OBS on 255, and fly it with a FROM flag
OBS on 075, and fly it with a FROM flag
questions.why: A radial is outbound from the station [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]], so you fly the 075 radial away from the VOR. Flying away from a station, use a FROM flag; otherwise the needle works backward [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]].

questions.q: You are lost at 1,500 ft AGL under an overcast at about 2,500 ft AGL. Your VOR shows a NAV flag. You are not instrument rated. What is the best move?
options: Climb through the overcast to get good VOR reception on top, since height improves reception
Climb only as far as you can while staying clear of the clouds, since height improves reception
Descend below the clouds to read road signs and town names and find a landmark you know
Turn back and search for your last checkpoint, since the VOR may work again there
questions.why: VOR signals are line-of-sight, so more height helps [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. A lost pilot should climb, but while watching traffic and weather [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Many non-instrument pilots lose control when they fly into clouds [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

questions.q: You will cross a town. The highest obstacle within 2,000 ft of your path is a tower charted as 1450 with (380) under it. What is the lowest altitude 14 CFR 91.119 allows here?
options: 1,380 ft MSL
1,950 ft MSL
2,450 ft MSL
2,070 ft MSL
questions.why: On the chart the top number is the MSL height of the top, and the number in parentheses is its height AGL [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]]. Over a congested area you need 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft: 1,450 + 1,000 = 2,450 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 2,070 is only 1,000 ft above the ground at the tower's base.

questions.q: You lay a pencil on the sectional: the diversion field is 3.5 inches from where you are. Winds give you 96 knots over the ground (TAS 115), and the engine burns 8 GPH. Which estimate do you write down?
options: About 12.5 minutes and 1.7 gallons
About 17.5 minutes and 2.3 gallons
About 15 minutes and 2.0 gallons
About 22 minutes and 2.9 gallons
questions.why: 1 inch = 6.86 NM, so 3.5 inches is about 24 NM [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Time = 24 ÷ 96 = 0.25 hr = 15 minutes; fuel = 0.25 × 8 = 2.0 gallons [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Using TAS gives the too-short 12.5 minutes; using 28 SM as if it were NM gives 17.5 minutes [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

questions.q: Far from any Class B or C airspace, you cruise at 10,500 ft MSL over a ridge where the ground is 8,500 ft MSL. Does 14 CFR 91.215 require a Mode C transponder at this spot?
options: Yes, it is required everywhere at and above 10,000 ft MSL
Yes, because you are more than 3,000 ft above sea level
No, because airspace at and below 2,500 ft AGL is left out of the 10,000-foot rule
No, because Mode C is only required inside Class B airspace
questions.why: Mode C is required at and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 states, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 ft above the surface [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]]. Here you are only 2,000 ft AGL. The ADS-B Out rule has the same exception [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]]. It is also required in Class B and C and in the Mode C veil, so 'only Class B' is wrong.

questions.q: You are lost at dusk. You have about 10 minutes of fuel left and no airport or open field in sight. Which call fits?
options: PAN-PAN, because being lost is only an urgency and you can still reach an airport
Wait until the engine quits, then call MAYDAY, so you do not alarm anyone too early
No call yet; squawk 7600 and keep looking for a field, since the radio is not needed
MAYDAY, because you are in serious, imminent danger and need help right now
questions.why: Distress means serious and/or imminent danger that needs immediate help [[34:337|P/CG Distress]]. Say MAYDAY three times; it has absolute priority and commands radio silence on the frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Being lost with plenty of fuel would be urgency, but low fuel while lost is very dangerous [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

questions.q: You plan a daytime trip of 1 hour 30 minutes at 8.5 GPH and take off with exactly the legal minimum fuel. A diversion adds 20 minutes of flying. About how much flying time is left in the tanks when you land?
options: About 10 minutes
About 25 minutes
About 30 minutes
None
questions.why: The day minimum is fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes at normal cruise [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151]]: 2.0 hr × 8.5 = 17 gallons. The flight now takes 1 hour 50 minutes, so only about 10 minutes remain. Plan to be on the ground before your planned fuel time runs out [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

questions.q: Diverting, you see on your FIS-B NEXRAD what looks like a gap in a line of storms between you and your alternate. How should you use that picture?
options: To fly through the gap, since the image is live and shows where the storms are right now
Only to plan a route that stays well clear of the whole area, not to pick a path through the gap
To fly through the gap, as long as the image is less than 5 minutes old and the gap is wide
Not at all, because FIS-B shows only TFRs and carries no weather radar returns at all
questions.why: FIS weather is for strategic decisions (20 minutes or more ahead), not tactical ones like finding a path through a weather hazard [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]. The actual weather can be up to 15 to 20 minutes older than the age shown [[1:329|PHAK 13-19]].

questions.q: Both your GPS and your VOR CDI needles are at full deflection while en route. About how far off course is each?
options: GPS: 12° or more; VOR: about 5 NM
GPS: about 5 NM; VOR: 12° or more
GPS and VOR: both about 10°
GPS: about 1 NM; VOR: about 6°
questions.why: En route, a GPS CDI shows distance: full scale is usually ±5 NM either side of the centerline [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]]. A VOR CDI shows angle: full deflection is 12° or more off course, about 2° per dot [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

questions.q: You are lost and calling for help. Besides your last known position, the time, and your heading since then, how does the AIM say to give your fuel?
options: In gallons remaining
As a percent of full tanks
In minutes of flying time remaining
In pounds remaining
questions.why: The AIM's distress and urgency message lists 'fuel remaining in minutes,' along with last known position, time and heading since that position if lost [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: Forty minutes after takeoff your checkpoints keep showing up off to one side. You have not touched the heading indicator since the runup. When and how should you check it against the compass?
options: Only on the ground, because the heading indicator does not drift in flight
During a turn, when the compass card is easiest to read and settles quickly
About every 15 minutes, while straight and level at a steady speed
Once an hour, while climbing at a steady speed with the nose held on a landmark
questions.why: Check the heading indicator about every 15 minutes and reset it to the compass when straight and level at a constant speed [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. The compass reads correctly only when its card is level, not in turns or speed changes [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

questions.q: On a clear afternoon you divert to an airport with a VOR on the field. Where is your midair collision risk highest?
options: Only if haze or darkness sets in and you lose sight of the airport
Only above 10,000 ft MSL, where you mix with faster aircraft
En route, far from any airport, where there are no navigation aids
Near that airport and its VOR, even in this clear weather
questions.why: Most midair collisions happen in good VFR weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport and/or near navigation aids [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. The PHAK says to be extra watchful near VORs and NDBs [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

questions.q: Inbound to a VORTAC at about 6,000 ft AGL, the needle swings and the flag flips from TO to FROM. About what does the DME show at that moment?
options: 0.0 NM, because you are over the station
About 6 NM, the same as your height
About 1 NM, because DME measures slant range
About 0.5 NM, half your height
questions.why: DME measures slant range, the straight-line distance to the station, so altitude counts. Directly over a VORTAC at 6,076 ft AGL it shows about 1.0 NM [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]] [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]]. The TO-FROM flip marks station passage [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]].

questions.q: You are climbing to improve radio reception while lost. The nose hides the sky ahead. How do you check that area for traffic?
options: Lower the nose now and then to see over it
Rely on ATC traffic calls
Climb steeper to get above traffic faster
Watch your traffic display instead of looking outside
questions.why: In a climb, adjust the pitch attitude to see over the nose and scan for traffic ahead [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. A lost pilot should climb while watching for traffic [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Traffic displays and ATC calls do not replace see-and-avoid [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].
